parts.title: Part I – Multiple Choice Questions
parts.instructions: Part I contains 75 questions. You must answer all of them. Each question carries 1 point. There is only one best answer for each question; blacken the letter of your choice on the Scantron answer sheet with a pencil.

parts.title: Part II – Work Out and Short Answer Questions
parts.instructions: Part II contains nine work out and short answer questions. You must answer all of them. This part carries twenty five points. Write your answers on the separate answer sheet provided.

All answers were solved independently, calculations were checked in Python (verify_calcs.py), and facts were checked against the Eritrean MoE Chemistry textbooks Grades 9–12. The Grade 11 PDF ends at p.129, so Gases (Unit 5) and the later part of Unit 4 (extraction of iron) are checked against standard chemistry only. See confidence and review_flag on each question.

questions.stem: Which of the following substances does not represent an alloy?
explanation_steps: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of a metal with other metals or with non-metals (textbook G9 p.26: brass, bronze, mild steel, stainless steel, solder).
Coins are made of alloys (e.g. cupronickel, brass), steel is iron + carbon, amalgam is mercury + another metal, and jewellery gold is alloyed with other metals for durability (G10 p.92).
Iron is a pure element, not an alloy. Answer: E.
tips: An alloy is a mixture, so it never has a single chemical symbol.

similar_questions.stem: Brass is an alloy of
explanation_steps: Brass = Cu + Zn; bronze = Cu + Sn. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter

additional_textbook_refs.section: 3.1 Solid solutions – gold alloys in jewellery

questions.stem: The number of periods in the modern Periodic Table is
explanation_steps: Each horizontal row of the periodic table is a period; the textbook states there are seven periods (G10 p.13).
There are 18 vertical columns (groups: 8 A-groups and 10 B-groups). Answer: C.
tips: 7 periods (rows), 18 columns (groups).

similar_questions.stem: An element with electron configuration 2, 8, 3 is in
explanation_steps: Three shells → period 3; three valence electrons → group IIIA (Al). Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2 The modern periodic table – periods and groups

questions.stem: Sodium hydroxide is used
explanation_steps: The textbook states that bases have important applications in the manufacture of soap (G10 p.130), and its exercise asks which substance can be made from NaOH – soap (G10 p.150).
Soap is made by boiling fats or oils with sodium hydroxide (saponification). Answer: C.
Alkaline batteries use KOH; antacids use Mg(OH)₂ or Al(OH)₃. NaOH is also found in drain and oven cleaners, so B is true in everyday life.
tips: NaOH (caustic soda) → hard soap; KOH → soft soap.

similar_questions.stem: Which base is commonly used as an antacid?
explanation_steps: Milk of magnesia, Mg(OH)₂, is a mild base that neutralises excess stomach acid. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: C (soap manufacture) is the textbook use, but NaOH is also a real household cleaner (drain and oven cleaner), so B is accepted as well.

questions.stem: The central part of an atom consists of
explanation_steps: The nucleus (the central part of an atom) contains protons and neutrons; electrons move around it in shells (G9 p.43). Answer: C.
tips: Nucleons = protons + neutrons.

similar_questions.stem: Which subatomic particle has no charge?
explanation_steps: The neutron is neutral. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 2 – Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding

questions.stem: The rates of reactions can be measured by noting the changes in

options.C: the loss or gain of mass.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.2): the rate of a reaction can be followed by measuring the volume of gas evolved, the loss or gain of mass, a change in colour, a change in pH, the change in temperature or the change in conductivity.
All four listed properties can be used. Answer: E.
tips: Choose any property that changes steadily as reactants turn into products.

similar_questions.stem: For CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ in an open flask, which measurement is most convenient for following the rate?
explanation_steps: CO₂ escapes, so the flask loses mass as the reaction proceeds. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting it
textbook_ref.section: 1.1.1 Measuring the rate of a chemical reaction

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of symbols is derived from an English name?
explanation_steps: Ar = argon and Al = aluminium – both come from the English names.
Na (natrium), K (kalium), Cu (cuprum), Au (aurum), Hg (hydrargyrum), Ag (argentum), Pb (plumbum) and Sb (stibium) come from Latin names (G9 p.80–83). Answer: B.
tips: If the symbol does not match the English name, it comes from Latin.

similar_questions.stem: Which symbol comes from the Latin name 'stannum'?
explanation_steps: Stannum = tin, Sn. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations

questions.stem: If a species accepts an electron in a redox reaction, it is
explanation_steps: Gain of electrons is reduction, so the species is reduced (B).
By accepting electrons it removes them from another species, causing that species to be oxidised – so it acts as the oxidising agent (C).
Both B and C are correct. Answer: E.
tips: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain. The oxidising agent is itself reduced.

similar_questions.stem: In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, the reducing agent is
explanation_steps: Zn loses electrons (is oxidised), so it is the reducing agent. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.section: 2.1 Oxidation and reduction; oxidizing and reducing agents

questions.stem: How many carbon atoms are joined in the spherical molecule of buckminsterfullerene?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.73): buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀, discovered in 1985, is a football-shaped (spherical) molecule of 60 carbon atoms. Answer: B.
tips: C₆₀ looks like a football: 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons.

similar_questions.stem: Which allotrope of carbon conducts electricity?
explanation_steps: Graphite has delocalised electrons between its layers. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds

questions.stem: Which of the following converts solar energy into chemical energy?
explanation_steps: Green plants such as a tree trap sunlight in photosynthesis and store it as chemical energy in glucose (G10 p.153, energy transformations).

A candle converts chemical energy into light and heat; a battery converts chemical into electrical energy; a bulb converts electrical into light and heat; the sun produces solar energy by nuclear fusion. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: A dry cell (battery) converts
explanation_steps: Redox reactions inside the cell produce an electric current. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 5.1 Energy transformations (Activity: plant, candle, light bulb)

questions.stem: Industrial chemistry deals with the

options.A: detection and monitoring of chemical substances in the air.
options.B: manufacturing of materials such as cement, glass and ceramics.
options.C: chemical processes that occur inside the cells of organisms.

explanation_steps: Industrial chemistry applies chemistry to the large-scale manufacture of materials such as cement, glass, ceramics, fertilisers and soap (G9 p.1–3).
A = environmental/analytical chemistry, C = biochemistry, D = organic chemistry, E = nuclear chemistry. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: The branch of chemistry that studies the chemical processes in living organisms is
explanation_steps: Biochemistry = chemistry of life. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter
textbook_ref.section: Introduction – branches of chemistry; chemistry and industry

questions.stem: The type of bond that is formed when non-metallic atoms share one or more pairs of valence electrons between them is called
explanation_steps: A covalent bond is formed by sharing pairs of valence electrons between non-metal atoms (G10 p.43).
Ionic bonds involve transfer of electrons (metal + non-metal); hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces are intermolecular attractions. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: How many shared electron pairs are there in an N₂ molecule?
explanation_steps: N≡N is a triple bond: three shared pairs. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction

questions.stem: The functional group that shows the presence of an organic acid is
explanation_steps: Textbook table of functional groups (G12 p.30): alcohols –OH, carboxylic (organic) acids –COOH, aldehydes –CHO, ketones –CO–, esters –COO–. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: The functional group of an aldehyde is
explanation_steps: Aldehydes contain –CHO. Answer: C.

questions.stem: An element X belongs to Period 3 and Group IA of the Periodic Table. What is the number of valence electrons in its atom?
explanation_steps: For A-group elements the group number equals the number of valence electrons: Group IA → 1.
Period 3 means three shells: 2, 8, 1 (sodium). Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: How many valence electrons does an element in period 2, group VIA have?
explanation_steps: Group VIA → 6 valence electrons (oxygen, 2,6). Answer: C.

questions.stem: The metal that is commonly used as electrical wire is
explanation_steps: Copper is the most commonly used metal for electrical wiring because it is an excellent conductor, ductile and relatively cheap.
Aluminium is used for overhead power lines because it is light, but household wiring and cables are mostly copper. Answer: E.
tips: Silver conducts best, but copper is the practical choice.

similar_questions.stem: Why is aluminium preferred for overhead power cables?

options.B: It is light and a good conductor
options.E: It has a very high density

explanation_steps: Low density plus good conductivity. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Chemistry of Some Metals and Their Compounds

questions.stem: Photosynthesis is an example of ______ reaction.
explanation_steps: Photosynthesis (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂) absorbs light energy; the products store more energy than the reactants.
A reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings is endothermic (textbook G10 p.164 lists producing sugar by photosynthesis as an energy-requiring process). Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which process is exothermic?
explanation_steps: Combustion releases heat. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The ability of a metal to be drawn into wires refers to its
explanation_steps: Ductility = ability to be drawn into wires; malleability = ability to be hammered into sheets (G10 p.52; G11 p.69). Answer: D.
tips: Ductile → wire; malleable → sheet.

similar_questions.stem: Gold can be beaten into very thin leaves. This property is
explanation_steps: Hammering into sheets = malleability. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction

questions.stem: The law that refers to the direct relationship between temperature and volume at constant pressure is
explanation_steps: Charles's law: at constant pressure the volume of a fixed amount of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (V/T = constant).
Boyle's law relates P and V at constant T; Avogadro's law relates V and moles. The ideal gas law PV = nRT contains the V–T relation but is not 'the law' of it. Answer: B.
tips: Charles: V ∝ T (P constant). Boyle: P ∝ 1/V (T constant). Gay-Lussac: P ∝ T (V constant).

similar_questions.stem: A gas occupies 2.0 L at 300 K. At constant pressure, what is its volume at 450 K?
explanation_steps: V₂ = V₁T₂/T₁ = 2.0 × 450/300 = 3.0 L. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Alkalis are

options.A: metals, which are soluble in water.
options.B: bases, which are insoluble in water.
options.C: acids, which are insoluble in water.
options.D: acids, which are soluble in water.
options.E: bases, which are soluble in water.

explanation_steps: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water (NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂) producing OH⁻ ions.
All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis (CuO, Fe(OH)₃ are insoluble). Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which of these bases is an alkali?
explanation_steps: KOH dissolves in water. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The gas laws apply to all of the following substances, except
explanation_steps: The gas laws describe the behaviour of gases. Oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide and ammonia are gases at ordinary conditions.
Gold is a solid metal, so the gas laws do not apply to it. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT behave according to the gas laws at room temperature?
explanation_steps: Mercury is a liquid at room temperature. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The following terms describe all crystalline solids, except
explanation_steps: Crystalline solids have particles in an orderly repeating pattern, giving definite geometric shapes, flat faces, straight edges and a definite coordination number (G12 p.13).
'Amorphous' means without regular arrangement – it describes non-crystalline solids such as glass. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which of these is an amorphous solid?
explanation_steps: Glass has no regular long-range arrangement. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals

questions.stem: Which of the following rays has the highest penetration power?
explanation_steps: Alpha particles are stopped by paper, beta particles by thin aluminium; gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation that need thick lead or concrete (G12 p.111–112). Answer: C.
tips: Penetrating power: α < β < γ; ionising power: α > β > γ.

similar_questions.stem: Which radiation is deflected most in an electric field and has a 2+ charge?
explanation_steps: Alpha particles are helium nuclei (2+). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Isotopes are atoms of one element with a different number of
explanation_steps: Isotopes have the same number of protons (same element) but different numbers of neutrons, hence different mass numbers (G9 p.47).
They differ in nucleons too (E), but that is a consequence of the different neutron number; the defining difference is neutrons. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: ¹²C, ¹³C and ¹⁴C differ in their number of
explanation_steps: 6, 7 and 8 neutrons respectively. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 2 – Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding

questions.stem: Which of the following is a promising potential biofuel that can be obtained by processing sugar cane, corn and other cereals?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.165, Did you know?): ethanol is a biofuel obtained from sugarcane, corn and other crops by fermentation.
Molasses is the raw material (a sugar syrup), not the fuel; petroleum is a fossil fuel. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Ethanol for fuel is produced from sugar by
explanation_steps: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ (yeast). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true about the ratio of the equilibrium quotient (Q) and the equilibrium constant (K) of a reversible reaction?

options.A: The product concentration becomes high if Q/K is greater than one.
options.B: The product concentration becomes low if Q/K is less than one.
options.C: The product concentration becomes low if Q/K is greater than one.
options.D: The net reaction proceeds to the left if Q/K is greater than one.
options.E: The net reaction proceeds to the right if Q/K is less than one.

explanation_steps: Q has the same form as K, [products]/[reactants], but with the actual concentrations (G11 p.20).
Q/K > 1 (Q > K): the product concentrations are higher than at equilibrium, so the net reaction goes to the left (A and D true).
Q/K < 1 (Q < K): the product concentrations are lower than at equilibrium, so the net reaction goes to the right (B and E true).
C contradicts A: when Q/K > 1 the products are high, not low. Answer: C.
Note: after the shift the products do decrease, so a reader who reads 'becomes' as the result of the shift could argue for A or B instead.
tips: Q > K → too much product → shift left. Q < K → too little product → shift right.

similar_questions.stem: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, K = 0.50. A mixture has Q = 0.10. The system will
explanation_steps: Q < K, so more NH₃ forms (shift right). Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting it

questions.review_flag: Wording 'becomes' is ambiguous: read as the state described by Q, C is the false statement (keyed); read as the result of the shift, A and B become false instead.

questions.stem: Which of the following compounds has the same molecular and empirical formula?
explanation_steps: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio. C₆H₆ and C₂H₂ → CH; C₆H₁₂O₆ → CH₂O; C₄H₁₀ → C₂H₅.
CH₄ cannot be simplified, so its empirical and molecular formulas are the same. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: The empirical formula of C₂H₄O₂ (ethanoic acid) is
explanation_steps: Divide by 2: CH₂O. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations

questions.stem: In the process of electroplating, the plating metal is the
explanation_steps: In electroplating the object to be plated is the cathode, the plating metal is the anode, and the electrolyte contains ions of the plating metal (G11 p.55, Activity 2.7).
The anode dissolves (e.g. Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻), replacing the ions that are deposited on the cathode. Answer: B.
tips: Object = cathode; plating metal = anode.

similar_questions.stem: To silver-plate a spoon, the spoon is made the
explanation_steps: Ag⁺ ions are reduced onto the cathode (spoon). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not correct about a pure substance? It has a
explanation_steps: A pure substance has a fixed, uniform composition and definite properties, including a sharp (fixed) melting point and boiling point (G9 p.11, p.20).
A variable melting point (melting over a range) indicates an impure substance or mixture. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: A sample melts gradually between 72 °C and 78 °C. This suggests the sample is
explanation_steps: Impurities lower and broaden the melting range. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter

questions.stem: ______ is the chemical formula of the salt used to treat anaemia.
explanation_steps: Textbook table of uses of salts (G10 p.143): FeSO₄·7H₂O – to treat anaemia; NaHCO₃ – baking powder; Na₂CO₃ – manufacture of glass and soap; NH₄NO₃ – fertiliser.
Iron(II) sulphate supplies iron for making haemoglobin. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which salt is used as a fungicide/pesticide?
explanation_steps: Copper sulphate is used as a pesticide and fungicide (G10 p.143). Answer: B.

questions.stem: The pH of a solution is 7, and its pH can be increased by

options.A: adding a small amount of an acid.
options.B: adding a small amount of a base.
options.C: adding a small amount of sulphuric acid.
options.D: adding a small amount of water.
options.E: passing carbon dioxide gas through it.

explanation_steps: pH 7 is neutral. Adding a base increases [OH⁻] and raises the pH above 7.
Acids, sulphuric acid and CO₂ (forms carbonic acid) lower the pH; water leaves a neutral solution at 7. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which change lowers the pH of pure water?
explanation_steps: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃, a weak acid. Answer: C.

questions.stem: A 48 g sample of a compound contains 12 g of carbon and 36 g of oxygen. What is the percentage composition of carbon and oxygen in the sample?

similar_questions.stem: A 20 g sample of a compound contains 8 g of calcium. What is the percentage of calcium?

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations

questions.stem: In the modern Periodic Table, elements are arranged horizontally in increasing order of their
explanation_steps: The modern periodic law: elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, i.e. the number of protons (G10 p.16).
Mendeleev used atomic masses; the modern table uses atomic numbers. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which scientist first arranged the elements by atomic number (from X-ray studies)?
explanation_steps: Henry Moseley (1913). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following substances does not have a fixed volume at standard temperature and pressure?
explanation_steps: Solids (sand, salt, wood) have fixed shape and volume; liquids (water) have a fixed volume but take the shape of the container.
Gases such as oxygen have neither fixed shape nor fixed volume – they fill their container. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which state of matter has a fixed volume but no fixed shape?
explanation_steps: Liquids flow but keep their volume. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter

questions.stem: The next member of C₈H₁₈ in the alkane homologous series is
explanation_steps: Alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and successive members differ by CH₂.
C₈H₁₈ + CH₂ = C₉H₂₀ (2 × 9 + 2 = 20). Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which formula belongs to the alkene series?
explanation_steps: Alkenes CₙH₂ₙ: C₄H₈. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following compounds of sulphur has not been found in Eritrea?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.100): compounds of sulphur such as pyrite (FeS₂), ZnS (zinc blende), CuFeS₂ (copper pyrite) and CuS have been found in parts of Eritrea, for example Debarwa and Adi Nefas.
Galena (PbS) is listed as a sulphur ore in general but not among those found in Eritrea. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Where has elemental (free) sulphur been found in Eritrea?
explanation_steps: The textbook names Marsa Fatuma and Erta Ale. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of elements and their valence electrons is not correct? [Atomic number: S = 16, Cl = 17, K = 19, Ca = 20 and Si = 14]
explanation_steps: Silicon has 4 valence electrons, not 3. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: How many valence electrons does phosphorus (Z = 15) have?
explanation_steps: 2, 8, 5 → 5 valence electrons. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 2 – Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding

questions.stem: The members of the alkene homologous series have the same
explanation_steps: A homologous series has the same general formula, the same functional group (C=C for alkenes) and similar chemical properties; physical properties such as density and state change gradually (G12 p.36).
Each member has a different molecular formula (C₂H₄, C₃H₆, …). Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Successive members of a homologous series differ by
explanation_steps: Each member adds a –CH₂– unit. Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following compounds are binary compounds, except
explanation_steps: Binary compounds consist of two elements: MgS, CaO, H₂O, NH₃.
Calcium sulphate, CaSO₄, contains three elements (Ca, S, O) – a ternary compound. Answer: C.
tips: -ide usually means binary; -ate/-ite means oxygen is also present.

similar_questions.stem: Which of these is a ternary compound?
explanation_steps: Na, C and O: three elements. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Chemical Symbols, Formulas and Equations
textbook_ref.section: 3.2 Naming and writing formulas for simple compounds

questions.stem: Which of the following metal oxides has an amphoteric property?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.123): metal oxides such as aluminium oxide and zinc oxide react with both acids and bases to give salts and water – amphoteric oxides.
BaO, CaO, Na₂O and K₂O are basic oxides. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Which oxide reacts with both HCl and NaOH?
explanation_steps: ZnO is amphoteric. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Chemistry of Some Metals and Their Compounds

questions.stem: Which of the following acids does not form an acidic salt?
explanation_steps: Acid salts form when only some of the replaceable hydrogen ions of an acid are replaced by a metal, so only polyprotic (dibasic or tribasic) acids form them (G10 p.140).
H₃PO₄ (NaH₂PO₄), H₂SO₄ (NaHSO₄), H₂CO₃ (NaHCO₃) and H₂SO₃ (NaHSO₃) all form acid salts.
HCl is monobasic (one replaceable H), so it forms only the normal salt, e.g. NaCl. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is an acid salt?
explanation_steps: NaHSO₄ still contains a replaceable H. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Intensive properties are

options.A: dependent on the amount of matter.
options.B: independent of the amount of matter.
options.C: independent of the type of matter.

explanation_steps: Intensive properties (density, melting point, boiling point, colour) do not depend on the amount of the sample; extensive properties (mass, volume) do (G9 p.14–15).
Intensive properties depend on the type of matter and are used to identify substances. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which is an extensive property?
explanation_steps: Mass depends on the amount of the sample. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of materials is not required during the separation of liquid mixtures by distillation?
explanation_steps: Simple distillation needs a distillation (round-bottom) flask, thermometer, condenser, receiver (conical flask), heat source, stand, clamp and tripod (G9 p.32).
A magnet separates magnetic solids (iron filings) and a hammer is not used at all. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: In distillation, the part that changes vapour back into liquid is the
explanation_steps: Cold water in the condenser cools the vapour. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about a heterogeneous mixture?

options.A: It consists of two or more elements that are physically mixed together.
options.B: It often retains many of the properties of its components.
options.D: It can be separated into its components by physical means.

explanation_steps: The textbook's characteristics of mixtures (G9 p.25–26): made of two or more substances physically combined; can be separated by physical means; often retains many properties of its components; has a variable composition.
All the statements describe a heterogeneous mixture (A is loose – components may be compounds too – but the setter copies the textbook list). Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a heterogeneous mixture?
explanation_steps: Sand does not dissolve; the parts are visible. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter

questions.stem: The enthalpy change of a chemical reaction can be found from the

options.A: boiling and melting point difference of products and reactants.
options.B: solubility difference of products and reactants.
options.C: heat content difference of products and reactants.
options.D: electrons lost and gained during a reaction.

explanation_steps: Enthalpy (H) is the heat content of a substance. The enthalpy change is ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) (G10 p.158). Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: If H(products) = 50 kJ and H(reactants) = 120 kJ, ΔH equals
explanation_steps: ΔH = 50 − 120 = −70 kJ (exothermic). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true about van der Waals forces? They

options.A: are weak attractive forces that hold molecules together.
options.B: involve an interaction between polar and nonpolar molecules.

explanation_steps: Van der Waals forces are weak intermolecular attractions: dispersion forces (even between non-polar molecules), dipole–dipole forces and dipole–induced dipole forces between polar and non-polar molecules (G10 p.53).
They are much weaker than ionic or covalent bonds, so 'very strong electrostatic attraction' is false. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: The forces between molecules of iodine (I₂) are mainly
explanation_steps: I₂ is non-polar, so only dispersion forces act. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The change that causes an expansion when matter converts from solid into liquid, and then from liquid into gas, is
explanation_steps: Heating (increasing temperature) gives particles more kinetic energy; they move further apart, so the solid melts and the liquid then boils, expanding at each stage (G9 p.10–13).
Decreasing temperature or increasing pressure has the opposite effect. Answer: C.
Lowering the pressure can also cause a liquid to boil, but the change of state sequence solid → liquid → gas is normally produced by heating.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true regarding halogens?

options.B: In their binary compounds, they have an oxidation number of −1.
options.C: Their outermost electronic configuration is ns² np⁶.
options.D: Their compounds with alkali and alkaline earth metals are generally ionic in nature.
options.E: Elemental halogens exist as diatomic molecules.

explanation_steps: Halogens (group VIIA) have seven valence electrons: outer configuration ns² np⁵. ns² np⁶ is the noble-gas configuration. Answer: C.
They are non-metals, exist as F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂, and form ionic halides with group IA and IIA metals.
B is true for metal halides; strictly, in oxides such as Cl₂O₇ chlorine is positive, but the intended false statement is C.

explanation_steps: Bromine is a red-brown liquid. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not correct about ideal gases or real gases?

options.A: Ideal gases obey all gas laws under all conditions of temperature and pressure.
options.B: Real gases obey the ideal gas equation.
options.C: In ideal gases, the force of attraction among the molecules is negligible.
options.D: In real gases, the force of attraction is not negligible at all temperatures and pressures.
options.E: Real gases obey all gas laws only at high temperature and low pressure.

explanation_steps: An ideal gas is one that obeys PV = nRT and all gas laws exactly under all conditions; its intermolecular attractions and molecular volumes are negligible (A and C true).

Real gases have attractions and finite molecular volume, so they deviate from the ideal gas equation – especially at high pressure and low temperature – and behave nearly ideally only at high temperature and low pressure (D and E acceptable).
B states without qualification that real gases obey the ideal gas equation, which is not correct. Answer: B.
tips: Real gases are most ideal when hot and at low pressure.

similar_questions.stem: Under which conditions does a real gas behave most like an ideal gas?
explanation_steps: Molecules are far apart and fast, so attractions matter little. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about graphite and diamond is true?

options.A: They have the same crystal structure.
options.B: They have the same degree of hardness.
options.C: They have the same electrical conductivity.
options.D: They can undergo the same chemical reactions.

questions.stem: The correct increasing order in the relative strength of intramolecular and intermolecular forces is

options.A: hydrogen bond < dispersion forces < covalent bond < ionic bond.
options.B: dispersion forces < hydrogen bond < covalent bond < ionic bond.
options.C: hydrogen bond < dispersion forces < ionic bond < covalent bond.
options.D: dispersion forces < covalent bond < hydrogen bond < ionic bond.
options.E: covalent bond < hydrogen bond < ionic bond < dispersion forces.

explanation_steps: Intermolecular forces are weaker than bonds: dispersion forces are the weakest, hydrogen bonds are the strongest intermolecular forces.
Intramolecular bonds (covalent, ionic) are much stronger. The order used in the textbook (G10 p.41–42) is dispersion < hydrogen bond < covalent < ionic. Answer: B.
(The relative order of covalent and ionic bonds depends on the example; only B puts the intermolecular forces correctly below both bonds.)

similar_questions.stem: Which is the strongest intermolecular force?
explanation_steps: The covalent bond is intramolecular; among intermolecular forces the hydrogen bond is strongest. Answer: C.

questions.stem: According to the traditional oxidation-reduction definition, which of the following is a reduction reaction?

options.A: When freshly cut potato is exposed to air
options.B: When magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid
options.C: When hydrogen is combined with sulphur to produce hydrogen sulphide
options.D: When oxygen reacts with magnesium metal to yield magnesium oxide
options.E: The corrosion of iron or rusting

explanation_steps: Traditional definitions: oxidation = addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen; reduction = removal of oxygen or addition of hydrogen (G11 p.27–28).
H₂ + S → H₂S: hydrogen is added to sulphur, so sulphur is reduced. Answer: C.
A, D and E are additions of oxygen (oxidation). B is best described by electron transfer (Mg is oxidised), not by the traditional oxygen/hydrogen definition.

explanation_steps: CuO loses oxygen. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about the atomic structures of ¹⁶O²⁻, ¹⁹F⁻ and ²⁰Ne? [Atomic number: O = 8, F = 9 and Ne = 10]

options.A: Each structure contains the same number of protons.
options.B: The sum of the neutrons in ¹⁹F⁻ and ²⁰Ne is 20.
options.D: The sum of the neutrons in all three species is 27.

explanation_steps: Protons: O 8, F 9, Ne 10 – different (A false).
Neutrons: ¹⁶O 16 − 8 = 8; ¹⁹F 19 − 9 = 10; ²⁰Ne 20 − 10 = 10. F + Ne = 20 (B true); all three = 28 (D false).
Electrons: O²⁻ 8 + 2 = 10; F⁻ 9 + 1 = 10; Ne 10 – isoelectronic (C true). Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which species is isoelectronic with Ne?
explanation_steps: Mg²⁺ has 12 − 2 = 10 electrons. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not correct about the oxidation number of atoms in their free or combined state?

options.A: The oxidation number of oxygen is usually −2.
options.B: The oxidation number of hydrogen is −1 in hydrides.
options.C: The oxidation numbers of alkali metals and alkaline earth metals are often +1 and +2, respectively.
options.D: The oxidation number of sulphur in the sulphate ion is −2.
options.E: The oxidation number of a free atom of an element is zero.

explanation_steps: In SO₄²⁻: x + 4(−2) = −2 → x = +6. So sulphur is +6, not −2. Answer: D.
The other statements are standard oxidation-number rules (G11 p.29–31): O usually −2; H −1 in metal hydrides (NaH); group IA +1, IIA +2; free elements 0.

questions.stem: All of the following options are correct about exothermic reactions, except that

options.A: the enthalpy of reactants is greater than the enthalpy of products.
options.B: the bond formation energy in products is greater than the bond breaking energy in reactants.
options.C: the change in enthalpy of the reaction is negative.
options.D: energy flows from the reaction to the surroundings.
options.E: the enthalpy of reactants is less than the enthalpy of products.

explanation_steps: In an exothermic reaction heat is released: H(reactants) > H(products), ΔH < 0, energy flows to the surroundings, and more energy is released forming bonds than is absorbed breaking bonds (G10 p.158–163).
E describes an endothermic reaction. Answer: E.

explanation_steps: Products have more enthalpy than reactants. Answer: B.

Answer the following questions on the basis of the atomic structure of an element.

Define atomic mass

questions.stem: Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction of aluminium with chlorine to form aluminium chloride. (2 points)
explanation_steps: Aluminium forms Al³⁺ and chlorine forms Cl⁻, so the formula of aluminium chloride is AlCl₃.
Unbalanced: Al + Cl₂ → AlCl₃. Chlorine atoms: 2 on the left, 3 on the right; the least common multiple is 6, so use 3Cl₂ and 2AlCl₃.
Then 2 Al atoms are needed on the left: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃ (Al 2 = 2, Cl 6 = 6).
marking_points: Correct formulas Al, Cl₂, AlCl₃ (1 point)
tips: Get the product formula right from the ion charges first, then balance by coefficients only.

similar_questions.stem: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of magnesium with oxygen.
explanation_steps: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ give MgO; balance oxygen with 2MgO, then Mg with 2Mg.

questions.stem:
A solution has 5.6 g of KOH in 500 g of water. [Atomic mass: H = 1, O = 16, K = 39] Calculate:
3.1 The molality of the solution. (2 points)
3.2 The freezing-point depression of the solution when the molal freezing-point constant (Kf) of water is 1.86 °C/m. (2 points)
explanation_steps: Molar mass of KOH = 39 + 16 + 1 = 56 g/mol; moles of KOH = 5.6 g ÷ 56 g/mol = 0.10 mol.
Mass of solvent = 500 g = 0.500 kg. Molality m = moles of solute ÷ kg of solvent = 0.10 ÷ 0.500 = 0.20 m.
Freezing-point depression ΔTf = Kf × m = 1.86 °C/m × 0.20 m = 0.372 °C (G10 p.105).

The solution freezes at about −0.37 °C. (Because KOH is an electrolyte giving K⁺ and OH⁻, the real depression is nearly double, about 0.74 °C; the textbook formula ΔTf = Kf·m is what the question expects.)
marking_points: 3.1: moles of KOH = 0.1 mol (1 point); molality = 0.2 m with unit (1 point)
3.2: formula ΔTf = Kf·m (1 point); 0.372 °C (1 point); allow follow-through from a wrong molality
Accept 0.744 °C if the student correctly applies i = 2 for KOH
tips: Molality uses kilograms of SOLVENT, not litres of solution.

similar_questions.stem: 11.7 g of NaCl (M = 58.5 g/mol) is dissolved in 250 g of water. Find (a) the molality, (b) ΔTf using Kf = 1.86 °C/m (ignore dissociation).

Consider the acid–base properties of solutions:

4.2 Bases have a pH value of ___(a)___ and acids have a pH value of ___(b)___. (1 point)
questions.answer: 4.1 (a) blue; (b) red. 4.2 (a) greater than 7 (7–14); (b) less than 7 (0–7).
explanation_steps: Acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue (G10 p.114–115).
On the pH scale 7 is neutral; acidic solutions have pH below 7 and basic solutions have pH above 7 (G10 p.144–146).
marking_points: ½ point for each blank: blue, red, above 7, below 7
tips: Acid → red, base → blue: 'BaBy' (Base Blue).

similar_questions.stem: A solution has pH 11. (a) Is it acidic or basic? (b) What colour does it turn red litmus?
explanation_steps: pH > 7 is basic; bases turn red litmus blue.

subparts.question: Two uses of aluminium and why
subparts.answer: Power cables; aircraft/cooking pots; light, good conductor, corrosion resistant

explanation_steps: A blast furnace is charged at the top (A) with iron ore (Fe₂O₃), coke (C) and limestone (CaCO₃).

Hot air blown in near the bottom (C) burns coke: C + O₂ → CO₂; CO₂ + C → 2CO. Carbon monoxide reduces the ore: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (the textbook notes CO is used as a reducing agent in the extraction of iron, G11 p.77).
Limestone decomposes (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂) and CaO removes sand: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (slag).
Waste gases leave near the top (B). Molten slag, which is less dense, floats on the molten iron and is tapped off higher (D); the molten iron is tapped from the very bottom (E).

Aluminium uses follow from its properties: low density, good conductivity, corrosion resistance (oxide layer), malleability and ductility – e.g. power cables, aircraft and vehicle parts, cooking utensils, food foil, window frames.
marking_points: 5.1: ½ point for each of A–E
D and E: accept slag and molten iron in either order – the diagram shows the two taps at almost the same level (teacher's discretion)
5.2: 1 point for each correct use (a, b); ½ point for a matching reason (c) – light, conductor, corrosion resistant
tips: In the furnace, slag floats on iron because it is less dense.

similar_questions.stem: Write the equation for the reduction of haematite by carbon monoxide in the blast furnace and state the role of limestone.
similar_questions.answer: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Limestone decomposes to CaO, which combines with sandy impurities (SiO₂) to form slag, CaSiO₃.
explanation_steps: CO is the reducing agent; CaO is a basic flux.

questions.stem:
All the gases in the three containers (I–III) have the same volume (5 L) and pressure (896 mm Hg) and are placed in the same room: I contains H₂, II contains N₂, III contains Cl₂. [Atomic mass: H = 1, N = 14, Cl = 35.5] (2 points)
6.1 Which container contains the greatest mass (in grams)?
6.2 The container with the least density of gas is ______.
questions.image_alt: Three identical 5 L cylinders labelled I, II and III, each at 896 mm Hg, containing H2, N2 and Cl2 respectively.
explanation_steps: Same volume, pressure and temperature (same room) → by Avogadro's law the containers hold equal numbers of moles (n = PV/RT).
Mass = n × molar mass, so the gas with the largest molar mass has the greatest mass: H₂ = 2, N₂ = 28, Cl₂ = 71 g/mol → Cl₂ (III).
Density = mass/volume; all volumes are 5 L, so the lightest gas, H₂ (I), has the least density.
marking_points: 1 point each: III / Cl₂; I / H₂
tips: Equal V, P, T → equal moles; then compare molar masses.

similar_questions.stem: Equal volumes of O₂, CO₂ and CH₄ are at the same temperature and pressure. Which sample has (a) the greatest mass and (b) the most molecules?
similar_questions.answer: (a) CO₂ (44 g/mol); (b) all have the same number of molecules.
explanation_steps: Avogadro's law: equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules.

questions.stem: List the two allotropes of sulphur and two properties of each. (3 points)
questions.answer: 7.1 Rhombic sulphur: (a) stable below 96 °C; (b) bright yellow, m.p. 113 °C, density 2.07 g/cm³ (octahedral crystals). 7.2 Monoclinic sulphur: (a) stable above 96 °C; (b) pale yellow, m.p. 119 °C, density 1.98 g/cm³ (needle-shaped crystals).

subparts.question: First allotrope and two properties
subparts.answer: Rhombic: stable below 96 °C; bright yellow / m.p. 113 °C / density 2.07

subparts.question: Second allotrope and two properties
subparts.answer: Monoclinic: stable above 96 °C; pale yellow / m.p. 119 °C / density 1.98

explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.101–102): sulphur exists in two main allotropic forms, rhombic and monoclinic; rhombic is stable at room temperature up to 96 °C and monoclinic at or above 96 °C.
Table 3.2: rhombic – bright yellow, m.p. 113 °C, density 2.07 g/cc; monoclinic – pale yellow, m.p. 119 °C, density 1.98 g/cc.
Both are made of S₈ ring molecules packed differently.
marking_points: ½ point for each allotrope name
½ point for each correct property (two per allotrope)
tips: 96 °C is the transition temperature between the two allotropes.

similar_questions.stem: What is the transition temperature of sulphur, and which allotrope is stable at room temperature?
explanation_steps: Rhombic sulphur is stable below 96 °C.

questions.stem:
Write down the IUPAC names of the following two structures, and draw cyclopentane. (3 points)
8.1 CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)=CH₂
8.2 C₆H₅–CH₂CH₃ (a benzene ring bonded to an ethyl group)
8.3 Draw the structure of cyclopentane.
questions.answer: 8.1 2-Methylbut-1-ene (2-methyl-1-butene). 8.2 Ethylbenzene. 8.3 Cyclopentane: five CH₂ groups joined in a ring (a pentagon), C₅H₁₀.
explanation_steps: 8.1: the longest chain containing the C=C has four carbons (CH₂=C–CH₂–CH₃). Number from the end nearest the double bond: C1=C2; the methyl group is on C2. Name: 2-methylbut-1-ene.
8.2: an ethyl group (–CH₂CH₃) attached to a benzene ring: ethylbenzene.
8.3: cyclopentane, C₅H₁₀, is five carbon atoms in a ring, each bonded to two hydrogens; drawn as a pentagon (each corner = CH₂).
marking_points: 1 point each: 2-methylbut-1-ene (accept 2-methyl-1-butene); ethylbenzene; correct five-membered ring with CH₂ groups (or skeletal pentagon)
8.1: ½ point if the locant of the double bond or methyl group is wrong
tips: For alkenes, the double bond takes the lowest locant, then the substituents.

similar_questions.stem: Name CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ and draw cyclohexane.
similar_questions.answer: 2-Methylbutane; cyclohexane is a six-membered ring of CH₂ groups (hexagon), C₆H₁₂.
explanation_steps: Longest chain 4 C, methyl on C2.

questions.stem: Given the equation: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890.4 kJ. How much energy is given off when 5.00 moles of CH₄ are burned? (2 points)
explanation_steps: The thermochemical equation shows that 1 mol CH₄ releases 890.4 kJ (G10 p.170).
Energy released = 5.00 mol × 890.4 kJ/mol = 4452 kJ.
marking_points: 4452 kJ with unit (1 point); accept −4452 kJ
tips: Heat scales with the number of moles in the equation.
